appraisal_events.evidence: « Vous voyez bien que si puisqu'il est antidreyfusard, me répondit Swann, sans s'apercevoir qu'il faisait une pétition de principe. Cela n'empêche pas que je suis peiné d'avoir déçu cet homme — que dis-je ! ce duc — en n'admirant pas son prétendu Mignard, je ne sais quoi. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann convicts the duc of antisemitism and then mocks him twice over — the sneering self-correction « que dis-je ! ce duc » ridicules his rank vanity, and « son prétendu Mignard » denies him any connoisseurship over his own picture. The narrator's aside about the petitio principii marks Swann's logic as circular without offering any defense of the duc, so the ridicule stands while its reasoning is lightly ironized.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Oui, elle est charmante. À mon avis, du reste, elle l'a été encore davantage quand elle s'appelait encore la princesse des Laumes. Son esprit a pris quelque chose de plus anguleux, tout cela était plus tendre dans la grande dame juvénile […] tous ces gens-là sont d'une autre race, on n'a pas impunément mille ans de féodalité dans le sang. Naturellement ils croient que cela n'est pour rien dans leur opinion. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann grants the narrator's claim of the duchesse's intelligence only to withdraw its force: her charm is dated to an earlier self, her wit has hardened, and she is finally absorbed into a caste whose opinions are dictated by inherited feudal blood without its members knowing it. The praise is real but subordinated to a determinist diminishment of her mind.

status_effects.explanation: In this exchange the duc is branded an antisemite, sneered at for needing his title pronounced, and shown to be wrong about the attribution of his own painting, with no counterweight offered.

Her acknowledged charm and intelligence are relativized: the best version of her is placed in the past, her wit is called more angular, and her opinions are attributed to caste rather than to judgment.

Swann answers both of the narrator's defenses of the Guermantes and closes the exchange with a sweeping diagnostic verdict on the whole caste; his command of the conversation is only lightly qualified by the narrator's note on his circular reasoning.

ambiguities: The narrator's aside « sans s'apercevoir qu'il faisait une pétition de principe » can be read either as a real undercut of Swann's authority as a judge or as a narrow logical caveat that leaves his verdicts standing; read here as the latter, so Swann's rhetorical gain is kept mildly positive rather than converted into a diminishment of him.

The closing generalization « tous ces gens-là sont d'une autre race, on n'a pas impunément mille ans de féodalité dans le sang » is poised between condemnation and a half-admiring recognition of aristocratic distinctness; the reading taken is that its explicit sequel about their unawareness of their own determination tips it downward for both Guermantes.
